extracted.intended_audience: students, critics, and readers of English poetry and literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and critical standards for assessing qualities of English poetry (style, melancholy, and treatment of nature), with attention to Celtic influences and distinctions between modes of handling nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Turn for style
rubrics_metrics.description: English poetry's 'turn for style' — a peculiar recasting and heightening of expression which adds dignity and distinction; a characteristic impulse in poetical races and epochs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page contrasts masters of style (Pindar, Virgil, Dante, Milton, Shakespeare) with literatures lacking this 'turn for style' (e.g., much German poetry). Style here is not merely idiomatic clarity but a pressure of emotion and sustained, heightened manner that gives special intensity to delivery. Examples: Milton passages vs Goethe; the Elizabethan style as continuation of Shakespeare's manner. Anti-pattern: confusing neat idiomatic or prose-like lucidity with this poetical 'style'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of style (effect = dignity and distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Power of style properly so-called has for its characteristic effect 'to add dignity and distinction' to what is said.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish this from 'idiomatic, simple, nervous, racy expression' (exemplified by Luther or Cobbett). Masters of style in prose (Cicero, Bossuet, Bolingbroke) and in poetry (Dante, Milton) exemplify this effect. When evaluating, ask whether phrasing transforms content into something more elevated and distinguished rather than merely clear or vigorous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetical simplicity versus prose simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: The simplicity of great poetry is a 'poetical' simplicity different from the simplicity of prose; simple passages in great poets are masterpieces of poetical simplicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Menander or Goethe may show prose-like simplicity, whereas Pindar, Dante, Shakespeare, and Milton achieve a simplicity that crowns a heightened poetic manner. Evaluate whether a 'simple' passage retains the special key or pitch of poetry rather than sliding into prosaic plainness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of handling nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Four distinct ways of handling nature in poetry: the conventional way, the faithful way, the Greek way, and the magical way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descriptions and examples provided: (1) Conventional: the eye is not on the object; clichéd eighteenth-century images ('As when the moon, refulgent lamp of night--') are examples to avoid. (2) Faithful: the eye is on the object and gives realistic, exact representation (example: many German pieces, Goethe's 'Zueignung' stanzas). (3) Greek: the eye is on the object but adds radiancy and brightness (examples: Theocritus, Keats lines 'What little town by river or seashore...'). (4) Magical: the eye is on the object but adds charm and magic — the Celtic 'natural magic' (examples: Celtic romance passages, Keats's 'magic casements'). When judging nature-painting, identify which mode is in play and whether the poet successfully adds the intended radiance or magic rather than falling into convention or mere faithful reportage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural magic / magical rendering of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'magically vivid and near interpretation of nature' — the fairy-like, intimate life of nature that imparts charm and wonder distinct from Greek radiance or German realism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Qualities: delicate tact, nearness to nature's secrets, vividness, fairy-charm. Examples from Celtic romance (flower-maiden, hawk/raven/snow comparisons), Shakespeare, Keats, Wordsworth, and Celtic place-names evoking lofty beauty. Anti-pattern: taking faithful realism or mere classical brightness for this magic; imitation by non-native literatures may lack the 'stamp of perfectness and inimitableness' found where it is native.

rubrics_metrics.name: Celtic contributions: style, melancholy, and natural magic
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim that English poetry owes (1) much of its turn for style, (2) much of its melancholy (Titanism), and (3) nearly all of its natural magic to Celtic sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence and examples: Celt poets' 'Pindarism' (intoxication of style), Ossian's influence on European melancholy, Llywarch Hen's passionate melancholy compared with Byron's Titanism. When evaluating English works for Celtic influence, look for heightened stylistic recasting, a violent/struggling melancholy (as distinct from German Sehnsucht), and intimate magical nature-painting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional/spiritual excitation as origin of style
rubrics_metrics.description: Style arises from a certain condition of spiritual excitement or pressure of emotion that recasts discourse into heightened and intense expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page emphasizes that the 'power of style' is produced under emotional urgency—an 'ever-surging, yet bridled, excitement' in the poet. In evaluation, consider whether stylistic effects feel organically driven by emotion or are merely decorative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity / native stamp versus imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Aesthetic qualities native to a people (e.g., Celtic natural magic) have a 'stamp of perfectness and inimitableness' that imitations elsewhere lack.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay warns that European literatures borrow and imitate, but where a gift is non-native, even when imitated it will lack the native perfection (examples: Novalis or Rückert may approach natural magic but may not equal authentic Celtic touches). When judging influence or merit, assess whether qualities feel original and native or derivative and imitative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of conventionalized nature-language
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of eighteenth-century conventionality: phrases where 'the eye is not on the object' are to be shunned as clichés.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of conventional, formulaic handling (e.g., 'As when the moon, refulgent lamp of night--' and many Latin conventionalisms). Evaluate descriptions of nature for immediacy and particularity rather than flattened, conventional epithet-lists.
